title: Rastorgueva’s Atlas of Tajik Dialects
text: This is a digitized version of the dialectal atlas of the Tajik language from the book An experience of the comparative study of Tajik dialects (Rus. Опыт сравнительного изучения таджикских говоров) by Soviet linguist Vera Rastorgueva (Расторгуева 1964) (read more). It contains 17 maps that show the distribution of a variety of linguistic features in around 100 settlements in modern-day Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, as well as a general map of dialect groups.

Reflexes of historical vowels *i, *ī
text:
Middle Persian front vowels *i, *ī have different reflexes in modern Tajik dialects:

*i → /i/; *ī → /i iː/. The two vowels remain separate phonemes. Nevertheless, in most dialects they are in clear opposition to each other only in open unstressed syllables. Attested in Falgar, Fergana, Matcha, Panjakent, Samarqand-Buxoro, Upper Chirchiq and Ūroteppa dialects.
*i, *ī → /i/. The two historic vowels have merged into one phoneme /i/. Attested in Badakhshan, Boysun, Derbent, Karategin, Kūlob, Near Panj, Qaratogh, Rogh, Vakhiyo-Darvoz and Varzob dialects.

Reflexes of historical vowels *u, *ū, *ō
text:
Middle Persian back vowels *u, *ū, *ō have different reflexes in modern Tajik dialects:

*u → /u uː/; *ū → /uː/; *ō → /ɵ/. All three vowels remain separate phonemes. The phoneme /uː/ is in clear opposition to /u/ only in open unstressed syllables. The phoneme /u/ is “unstable” and may be omitted in open unstressed syllables. The pronunciation of the phoneme /ɵ/ differs in quality across dialects, but on average it is more back than /ɵ/ in Near Panj dialects. Attested in Buxoro, East Fergana, Panjakent, Ūroteppa and West Fergana dialects and in some Falgar varieties.
*u, *ū → /u/; *ō → /ɵ/. Historically long *ū and short *u have merged into one phoneme /u/. The phoneme /uː/ is in clear opposition to /u/ only in open unstressed syllables. The phoneme /u/ is “unstable” and may undergo total reduction in open unstressed syllables. The pronunciation of the phoneme /ɵ/ differs in quality across dialects. Attested in Boysun, Derbent, Qaratogh, Samarqand and Varzob dialects.
*u, *ū → /y/; *ū, *ō → /uː/. In most cases, historically long *ū has changed into /y/ (merging with short *u), but in some words *ū has retained its vowel quality and changed into /uː/ (thus merging with *ō). The pronunciation of the phoneme /y/ differs in quality across dialects, specifically in backness. Attested in Matcha, North Fergana, South Fergana dialects and in some Falgar varieties.
*u → /ɯ/; *ū, *ō → /uː/. The historic vowels *ū and *ō have merged into one phoneme /uː/. The pronunciation of the phoneme /ɯ/ has various allophones and may undergo fronting, labialization or reduction depending on the phonetic context. Attested in Badakhshan, Karategin, Kūlob, Vakhiyo-Darvoz dialects and in some Near Panj varieties. According to Rastorgueva’s description, this type is also attested in some Varzob and Hisor varieties, but this is not reflected on her map.
*u → /ɯ/; *ū → /y/; *ō → /ɵ/. All three vowels remain separate phonemes, but with significant changes in quality. These varieties also have the phoneme /uː/, which in most cases is the result of change from the Middle Persian *ā before nasals. In some words of high register, mostly of Arabic origin, there is /uː/ that goes back to *u or *ū. The pronunciation of the phoneme /ɵ/ differs in quality across dialects, but on average it is more front than /ɵ/ in northern dialects. Attested in Near Panj dialects.

title: About
text:
In 1964, Soviet linguist Vera Rastorgueva (Rus. Вера Расторгуева) published her book An experience of the comparative study of Tajik dialects (Rus. Опыт сравнительного изучения таджикских говоров)1. This work proposed a new approach to classifying dialects of the Tajik language in the Tajik and Uzbek Soviet republics (modern-day Tajikistan and Uzbekistan).
Since the early 20th century, there was an idea in Russian and Soviet Iranian studies that Tajik dialects can be divided into two main dialect groups (this view was expressed, for example, by Petr Kuznetsov (1915) and Mikhail Andreev (1930)). However, according to Rastorgueva, over time it became clear that this classification was imperfect and did not reflect the true complexity of dialectal differences within the Tajik language. For example, the existence of the Varzob dialect, which displays both northern and southern features, led Rastorgueva to propose the existence of a third, “central” dialect group. Nevertheless, even with this correction, the isoglosses of various linguistic phenomena considered key to the definition of dialect groups often did not coincide, which led scholars to identify smaller subgroups within the major dialect groups. Rastorgueva’s 1964 book, An experience of the comparative study of Tajik dialects, systematized and expanded on the accumulated knowledge in this field. In particular, the dialect classification proposed in this book has become mainstream in Tajik dialectology and has been repeated in various overviews on this topic (Ефимов 1982: 12; Windfuhr 2009: 420–421).
Vera Rastorgueva suggested that four main dialect groups should be distinguished in the Tajik language: (a) northern, (b) central (Upper Zarafshon), (c) southern, and (d) southeastern (Darvoz). The key linguistic feature by which these groups can be easily distinguished is the reflexes of the Middle Persian back vowels *u, *ū, *ō (see map). According to Rastorgueva, these vowels are very common in Tajik words and are therefore clearly noticeable upon first encountering a particular dialect. Furthermore, she notes, this classification is indirectly confirmed by other linguistic phenomena: the verb system, certain syntactic features (for example, the left-branching possessive construction, various infinitive and participial constructions, the use of the archaic past participle to express future tense), and lexicon.
Each group can be divided into dialects (диалекты), which, in turn, are divided into smaller varieties (говоры) and sub-varieties (подговоры). The isoglosses of different dialectal phenomena usually do not coincide, so the identification of dialects and varieties can only be made based on specific combinations of isoglosses. The boundaries between individual dialects are unclear, as the dialects gradually merge into one another.
Rastorgueva divides the four groups into the following dialects:

Northern group

Samarqand-Buxoro
Samarqand-Jewish2
West Fergana
East Fergana
Ūroteppa
Urban Panjakent
Rural Panjakent
Varzob-Hisor3
Boysun
Derbent

Central group (Upper Zarafshon)

Matcha
Falgar

Southern group

Karategin
Rogh
Northern Kūlob
Southern Kūlob
Badakhshan

Southeastern group (Darvoz / Near Panj dialects)4

The above-mentioned groups also do not include “transitional” dialects that combine features of several dialects:

“Transitional” dialects between the central and northern groups (vocalism of the central type, verb system and syntax of the northern type)

Upper Chirchiq
North Fergana
South Fergana

“Transitional” dialects between the southern and southeastern groups (vocalism of the southern type, verb system of the southeastern type)

Vakhin-Darvoz (Vakhio-Bolin)

title: About
text:
Footnotes


This page is an overview of the general information about Tajik dialects and their classification from (Расторгуева 1964: 154–162).↩︎
Samarqand-Jewish dialect is not mentioned on the general map of dialect groups (Расторгуева 1964: 182).↩︎
Rastorgueva mentions Varzob-Hisor dialect, which includes Varzob, Mountain Hisor and Qaratogh varieties, in the overview (Расторгуева 1964: 159). On the general map of dialect groups (Расторгуева 1964: 182), however, the settlement of Hisor is not given any label, implying that its dialect group is not yet defined, and there is no Hisor dialect in the legend.↩︎
The internal classification of the Southeastern group, according to Rastorgueva, had not been determined at the time of her book’s publication. Efimov et al. (1982: 12) later identified the following varieties in this group (names preserved from the source): (1) the variety of the Jorf village; (2) the variety of villages Kyrgovat, Poshkharv; (3) the variety of villages Umarak, Zing; (4) the Sediya variety (villages Sangovi Daroz, Durobak, Patkinou); (5) the Shekai variety (villages Shergovat, Yagid, Shkev, Ravnou).↩︎

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
For a few years now, it has become very to create interactive maps with R thanks to the package leaflet by the Rstudio team. Nevertheless, it only provides only a few functions to create basic shapes on a map, so the information that can be represented on a single map is limited: if you have some data associated to some points, you can only represent at most two variables by drawing circles and changing their radius and color according to data.
leaflet.minicharts is an R package that provides two functions to add and update small charts on an interactive maps created with the package leaflet. These charts can be used to represent as many variables as desired associated to geographical points. Currently, three types of chart are supported: barcharts (the default), pie charts and polar area charts.
let’s have a look to a concrete example.

text:

The package provides a table that contains the electric production, consumption and exchanges of France from january 2010 to february 2017 and of 12 french regions from january 2013 to february 2017.

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
Renewable productions in 2016
Nowadays, France has an objective of 23% of renewable energies in the consumption of the country by 2020. Are the country close to its objective. Is the share of renewable energies similar in all regions?
To answer this question let us focus on the year 2016 We first prepare the required data with package dplyr:

We also create a base map that will be used in all the following examples
We now add to the base map a pie chart for each region that represents the share of renewable energies. We also change the width of the pie charts so their area is proportional to the total production of the corresponding region.






We can see that the three south east regions exceed the target of 23%, but most regions are far from this objective. Globally, renewable energies represented only 19% percent of the production of 2016.
Now let’s represent the different types of renewable production using bar charts.






Hydraulic production is far more important than solar and wind. Without surprise, solar production is more important in south while wind production is more important in the north.

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
Representing a single variable
leaflet.minicharts has been designed to represent multiple variables at once, but you still may want to use it to represent a single variable. In the next example, we represent the total load of each french region in 2016. When data passed to addMinicharts contains a single column, it automatically represents it with circle which area is proportional to the corresponding value. In the example we also use the parameter showLabels to display rounded values of the variable inside the circles.






This is nice, isn’t it?

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
Animated maps
Until now, we have only represented aggregated data but it would be nice to create a map that represents the evolution over time of some variables. It is actually easy with leaflet.minicharts. The first step is to construct a table containing longitude, latitude, a time column and the variables we want to represent. The table eco2mix already has all these columns. We only need to filter the rows containing data for the entire country.
Now we can create our animated map by using the argument “time”:

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
Represent flows
Since version 0.2, leaflet.minicharts has also functions to represent flows between points and their evolution. To illustrate this, let’s represent the evolution of electricity exchanges between France and Neighboring countries.
To do that, we use function addFlows. It requires coordinates of two points for each flow and the value of the flow. Other arguments are similar to addMinicharts.






Of course, you can represent flows and minicharts on the same map!

title: Introduction to leaflet.minicharts
text:
Use in shiny web applications
In shiny applications, you can create nice transition effects by using functions leafletproxy and updateMinicharts/updateFlows. In the server function you first need to initialize the map and the minicharts. The important thing here is to use parameter layerId so that updateMinicharts can know which chart to update with which values.
